answers.rationale: History supports choosing between taxi and rideshare based on live wait, traffic, weather, luggage, and child logistics rather than using rideshare as a fixed default. With storms, a child, two roller bags, and a transit transfer plus walk, transit should not be the primary plan; taxi versus rideshare can be decided on arrival.

Maya has used rail when it is directly useful and conditions support it, while retaining rideshare as a weather, disruption, or timing fallback. A station-adjacent downtown hotel and slow freeway traffic make MAX the sensible primary choice, but the dinner reservation warrants monitoring and a switch if the buffer erodes.

For short no-car family trips, history consistently treats the closer airport as the baseline but evaluates alternates against total savings, transfer cost, arrival timing, and family friction. It does not support automatically choosing either the nearest airport or the cheapest nonstop. MIA should lead unless FLL remains materially better after those factors are priced.

The history favors nonstops and workable arrival windows when a connection creates meaningful schedule risk, while not treating proximity as absolute. Here IAH is far cheaper, arrives midafternoon, and avoids a late connection; its longer but straightforward solo rideshare is the better tradeoff than Hobby.
